title: AI usage: Topic and interaction need separate measurement
desc: Provides a weighted classification framework for professional and personal assistance while preserving uncertainty and reporting no trend.

kps.k: The cluster contributes a framework for measuring requested AI assistance, not evidence of productivity or displacement.
kps.d: How People Use ChatGPT and OpenAI Signals classify what users request rather than what ChatGPT successfully delivers. Their shared distinction separates Asking for information or decision support, Doing through primarily model-created output, and Expressing without either request. This helps distinguish advice-seeking from task delegation, but delegation alone does not establish autonomous execution, reliance without human verification or replacement of workers. The supplied material presents no substantive disagreement or measured effects.

kps.k: Topic and interaction type provide distinct dimensions of use, spanning professional and non-professional activity.
kps.d: How People Use ChatGPT groups 24 categories into Writing, Practical Guidance, Technical Help, Multimedia, Seeking Information, Self-Expression and Other/Unknown. OpenAI Signals elaborates distinctions such as editing supplied text versus generating arguments or summaries, alongside programming, teaching, everyday advice and social interaction. Analysts can use this granularity to avoid treating all usage as generic work assistance. Neither the category list nor its repetition across the materials establishes the prevalence of any activity.

kps.k: Work-related classification depends on contextual inference and must preserve uncertainty.
kps.d: OpenAI Signals uses team audiences, professional tone, raise advice and client correspondence as cues to professional use. These worked examples illustrate plausible classification rather than confirm facts about observed users. The taxonomy also separates unclear intent from a clear request outside its listed capabilities. Practically, analysts should distinguish inferred work context, ambiguous intent and taxonomy gaps rather than collapse them into a single residual category.

kps.k: The sampling design supports weighted, smoothed usage comparisons, but the supplied excerpts report no numerical trend.
kps.d: How People Use ChatGPT describes approximately 1.1 million sampled conversations from May 15, 2024 to June 26, 2025, reweighted to daily message volumes and averaged over a trailing 28-day window. Its chart distinguishes users who first adopted ChatGPT during or before Q2 2024 from successive quarterly cohorts. These details explain how the chart constructs comparisons; they do not establish adoption rates, changes in task mix, productivity gains or causal effects.

vlens.an: The legal-tech-vendor sources in this curated cluster support the proposition that AI usage should be measured along separate topical and interaction-type dimensions and that such classifications describe requested assistance rather than demonstrated performance, productivity or worker displacement. Their common basis is methodological: both distinguish advice-seeking (“Asking”), model-produced task output (“Doing”) and non-task expression, while classifying the requested capability separately. Material variation is complementary rather than conflicting. How People Use ChatGPT adds the sampling architecture—daily-volume reweighting, 28-day smoothing and cohort comparisons—whereas OpenAI Signals provides more detail on capability categories, contextual inference of professional use, and the separation of unclear intent from requests outside the taxonomy. Neither source, on the supplied evidence, reports a numerical trend or treats task delegation as autonomous execution or substitution. Because these are closely related OpenAI materials from a curated selection, their agreement should not be interpreted as representing legal-tech vendors generally.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition. It explicitly measures requested capabilities and separately classifies interaction mode as Asking, Doing or Expressing, so topic and type of assistance are not conflated. Its sampling discussion also supports the proposition’s methodological restraint: the excerpts describe a large conversation sample, daily-volume reweighting, 28-day smoothing and cohort construction, but do not report a numerical adoption trend or establish productivity, autonomous execution, worker displacement or causal effects. There is no material internal disagreement in the supplied source evidence. The main variation is between its substantive classification framework and its sampling methodology; both remain measurement contributions rather than evidence of outcomes. Because this is one source from a curated corpus, its position should not be treated as representative of a broader group.

elens.an: The current-wave source, OpenAI Signals, supports the proposition that topic and interaction need separate measurement. It distinguishes interaction intent—such as advice-seeking, task delegation and expression—from the capability or topic requested, and it separately retains “unclear” intent and capabilities falling outside the taxonomy. This directly reinforces the cluster’s methodological framing while remaining limited to classification: it does not report adoption trends, successful task completion, productivity effects, autonomous execution or worker displacement. There is no substantive internal disagreement in the supplied record; the material variation is between classifying interaction type, classifying capability, and inferring professional context from qualified contextual cues. Because this is a single curated source record, its position should not be generalized to all current-wave sources.
